Speculative decoding accelerates inference by having a cheap draft model propose token sequences that the target model verifies in parallel, with the acceptance rate α — the fraction of draft tokens accepted per step — determining the realized speedup; when α falls below roughly 0.6–0.7, the overhead of running both models erases the latency gain. The central question here is: when the draft and target models were pretrained on meaningfully different corpora (different domain mixtures, different language distributions, different temporal windows), how does the token-level conditional distribution divergence translate into α collapse, and under what conditions does that collapse become catastrophic rather than merely degrading? Key concepts are the token-level acceptance criterion (draft token x accepted with probability min(1, p_target(x|context)/p_draft(x|context))), corpus-induced KL divergence in the conditional distributions, and the compounding effect of sequential rejections — a single rejection resets the sequence, so even modest per-token divergence compounds multiplicatively across the speculation window. What a beginner misses is that α collapse is not uniform across context types: it is context-triggered and bimodal — the draft model may perform acceptably on generic prose but catastrophically on domain-specific terminology, code-switching passages, or temporal references post-dating the draft's training cutoff, meaning aggregate α statistics mask localized failure modes that appear only under specific input distributions. The expert worry is that naive corpus audit metrics (vocabulary overlap, perplexity ratios) do not predict which specific conditional distributions will diverge worst, because the problem is not about marginal token frequency but about high-order conditional probability mass allocation in long-tail contexts.

The geometry of divergence maps onto collapse phenotype through a simple but underappreciated mechanism: high-frequency token divergence (function words, punctuation, common subwords) produces chronic attrition because these tokens appear in nearly every window, so even a 10–15% per-token rejection elevation aggregates across the 4–8 token speculation depth to devastate α multiplicatively — a 0.85 per-token acceptance on a depth-6 window yields α ≈ 0.38, well below the break-even threshold. Low-frequency divergence concentrated in rare domain tokens (e.g., medical terminology, code identifiers, post-cutoff named entities) produces the catastrophic reset pattern: most windows proceed normally until a trigger token appears, at which point p_target/p_draft collapses toward zero and the entire window is rejected, wasting all draft compute. Leviathan et al. (2023), the original speculative decoding paper, measured α in the 0.7–0.9 range on matched-distribution benchmarks but did not systematically characterize what happens when the draft encounters out-of-distribution lexical items — the implicit assumption was corpus alignment. In practice, systems like Medusa and Eagle (which train draft heads on the target model's own activations) partially sidestep this by anchoring draft distributions to target internals, but externally trained draft models (e.g., a 7B paired with a 70B from different pretraining runs) are fully exposed to both failure modes simultaneously. The critical expert insight is that high-frequency divergence is actually harder to fix: you can augment domain vocabulary with continued pretraining on the draft, but restructuring how the draft allocates probability mass over function words and common subwords requires retraining at a scale that defeats the cost motivation for using a small draft model in the first place. Empirically, Chen et al.'s SpecBench evaluations show α variance across task types exceeding 0.3 absolute even among nominally matched model families, with the worst degradation on tasks demanding precise syntactic continuations — consistent with high-frequency structural token divergence rather than lexical.

Tokenizer-induced misalignment is a genuinely distinct failure mode: when draft and target use different vocabularies or different BPE merge sequences, the same surface string maps to non-isomorphic token sequences, making the standard token-level acceptance criterion (min(1, p_target/p_draft)) formally undefined or meaningless — you are comparing probability mass over incomparable discrete spaces. The cleanest fix is to lift verification from token space to character- or byte-span space: rather than comparing p_target(token_k) to p_draft(token_k), you marginalize both models over all tokenizations of the next n characters and compare those span-level probabilities, which is tokenizer-agnostic by construction. This is the core idea behind universal speculative decoding (Sun et al., 2024), which proposes operating over byte-level spans to enable cross-tokenizer speculation — their experiments show that naive token-level verification between mismatched vocabularies inflates effective rejection rates by 20–40% relative to the true distributional divergence, meaning a substantial fraction of observed α collapse in cross-family model pairings is tokenizer artifact rather than semantic mismatch. A cheaper diagnostic is fertility ratio monitoring: if the draft tokenizer consistently segments a context window into more tokens than the target tokenizer would (higher fertility), the positional mismatch itself generates spurious rejections because draft token k does not correspond to target token k even when the underlying probability over surface strings is nearly identical. Systems like Medusa avoid this entirely by sharing the target's tokenizer for draft head prediction, but externally paired models (LLaMA-family draft with Mistral-family target, for instance) cannot assume vocabulary alignment and must either retokenize on the fly or accept inflated false rejection rates. The practical diagnostic protocol an expert would run first is a controlled fertility audit: hold the input fixed, tokenize with both vocabularies, and measure position-wise token boundary agreement — divergence exceeding 5–10% boundary mismatch at any position is sufficient to contaminate the entire downstream speculation window regardless of true probability alignment.

The net-positive condition for cross-tokenizer speculative decoding with byte-span marginalization hinges on three architectural parameters: the ratio of draft-to-target inference cost (β), the expected number of tokenization paths that must be enumerated per span (the lattice width λ), and the achieved α after correction — the speedup formula generalizes to roughly (1 - α^(γ+1)) / ((1 - α)(1 + β·λ·γ)) where γ is speculation depth, making it immediately visible that λ enters multiplicatively with β, so even a cheap draft becomes net-negative if the tokenization lattice is wide. Lattice width is determined primarily by vocabulary overlap structure: when both tokenizers are BPE-derived from similar corpora, most spans have only 1–3 valid tokenizations and λ stays manageable, but when one tokenizer is byte-level (e.g., ByT5-style) and the other is word-piece, λ can grow exponentially with span length, making marginalization over spans longer than 3–4 characters computationally intractable without aggressive pruning. The provably not-worth-doing regime is characterized precisely: when β < 0.1 (very cheap draft) but λ > 8, the marginalization overhead consumes more wall-clock time than the parallel verification saves, and since α after correction is bounded above by the true distributional alignment (which may itself be poor for cross-family models), you cannot compensate with deeper speculation without hitting the exponential lattice growth problem simultaneously. Empirically, Sun et al. (2024) report that cross-tokenizer speculative decoding is net-positive only when span length is capped at 2–3 characters and lattice enumeration is pruned to the top-k paths by draft probability mass — unconstrained marginalization on spans of 6+ characters produced slowdowns of 1.3–1.8× relative to target-only inference in their ablations. A further architectural constraint is KV cache reuse: standard speculative decoding amortizes target model cost by reusing the KV cache across the verified prefix, but when retokenization changes token boundaries, the cached keys and values are positionally invalidated, forcing partial recomputation that compounds the marginalization overhead. The regime where cross-tokenizer speculation is structurally unviable — not just empirically poor — is when the target model uses rotary position embeddings (RoPE) with absolute token-index encoding and the retokenization shifts token positions by more than 1–2 slots, because the position-dependent attention patterns are no longer transferable across the boundary shift, making KV cache reuse formally incorrect rather than merely approximate.

The root cause of cache invalidity is that RoPE and ALiBi both encode position as a function of token index rather than character or byte offset, so any retokenization that shifts token count — even by one — corrupts every downstream attention score that depends on relative position, making the cached KV tensors from the original tokenization incorrect for the new token sequence. The minimum architectural change that achieves cache consistency under boundary shifts is to anchor position encodings to byte offsets rather than token indices: each token's position embedding is computed from the byte position of its first character in the original string, making the encoding invariant to how that string is segmented into tokens. This is precisely the design choice in character-aware transformers like CANINE (Clark et al., 2022) and the byte-level models in MegaByte (Yu et al., 2023), where position is a property of the input stream rather than the tokenization — in MegaByte's architecture, the global model operates over fixed-size byte patches with patch-position encoding, which is trivially cache-consistent across any sub-patch tokenization variation. A less invasive modification for existing RoPE models is span-anchored RoPE: instead of assigning position i to the i-th token, assign position based on cumulative byte length of the prefix, interpolating RoPE frequencies accordingly — this requires no changes to attention kernel structure, only to the position index computation, and preserves cache validity as long as the byte-span prefix is unchanged even when internal segmentation shifts. The practical barrier is that span-anchored RoPE has not been validated at scale in any publicly released model, and the frequency interpolation introduces small but nonzero perturbations to attention patterns relative to standard RoPE, meaning you cannot simply retrofit it onto a pretrained model without fine-tuning to recalibrate the position-dependent components — Su et al.'s original RoPE paper and the subsequent YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) length-extrapolation work both show that even small changes to position frequency scaling require thousands of fine-tuning steps to restabilize perplexity. The minimum viable path that avoids retraining entirely is a hybrid cache strategy: maintain two KV caches, one indexed by token position (used for generation) and one indexed by byte offset (used for speculative verification), recomputing only the misaligned suffix when boundary shifts occur — this adds memory overhead of roughly 1.5–2× the standard KV cache size but requires zero architectural change to the underlying model, making it deployable against frozen pretrained weights.

Span-anchored position encodings do create a genuine semantic collision risk, but the mechanism is more subtle than simple byte-length equivalence: the collision occurs specifically when two morphologically distinct token sequences have identical byte-offset profiles for their constituent tokens, causing the position signal to contribute identically to attention score computation while the token embedding signal must carry the entire burden of disambiguation — effectively concentrating all semantic differentiation into the embedding lookup and removing the positional co-signal that standard models use to resolve local ambiguity. In standard RoPE models, position index and token identity jointly determine the query-key dot product, so even semantically similar tokens at different positions produce distinguishable attention patterns; under span-anchored RoPE, two sequences like "un|safe" (2 tokens, byte offsets 0,2) and "uns|afe" (2 tokens, byte offsets 0,3) have different offset profiles and are fine, but "cat" (1 token, offset 0–2) and "cat" represented as "c|at" after retokenization share the same span and produce attention patterns that differ only through embedding-path contributions, not position-path contributions. CANINE's evaluation (Clark et al., 2022) is instructive here: on morphologically rich languages like Finnish and Turkish, character-position-anchored models showed 2–4% accuracy degradation on tasks requiring disambiguation of morphologically similar surface forms compared to token-indexed baselines, which the authors attribute precisely to the position signal failing to differentiate tokens that occupy similar character spans. The new error class this creates is what might be called positional aliasing: the model cannot use attention head specialization that relies on position-token co-occurrence statistics learned during pretraining, because those statistics were built under token-indexed positions — retrofitting span-anchored encoding onto a pretrained model without retraining means the attention heads are operating under a position scheme they never saw during weight optimization. This matters most for tasks where syntactic role correlates with both position and morphology simultaneously — subject-verb agreement across long spans, for instance — because the model's learned heuristic for "token at relative position +3 is likely a verb" breaks down when position is byte-anchored and morphological segmentation varies. Empirically, MegaByte partially escapes this problem by operating with a two-level architecture where the local model sees token-level structure within patches while the global model sees patch-level byte positions, effectively preserving token-identity disambiguation within a bounded window while achieving byte-offset consistency at the inter-patch level — a design choice that looks, in retrospect, like an implicit solution to the positional aliasing problem even if it was not framed that way in the original paper.

The information-theoretic argument is precise and damning: in a token-indexed model, the effective information available to disambiguate token identity at position i is I(token) + I(position|context), where the positional co-signal contributes mutual information with the semantic target that is non-zero whenever position correlates with syntactic role — removing that co-signal forces the embedding alone to carry I(token) + I(position|context) worth of disambiguation, requiring the embedding space to expand to compensate. A concrete lower bound follows from a channel capacity argument: if the positional co-signal contributes H_pos bits of task-relevant information on average (estimable from how much attention head accuracy degrades when position encodings are ablated), then the embedding dimensionality must increase by at least H_pos / log2(1 + SNR) dimensions to recover equivalent resolution, where SNR is the signal-to-noise ratio of the embedding lookup — for typical transformer SNR values and positional ablation results showing 5–15% attention accuracy drops, this implies a 15–40% dimensionality inflation as a theoretical floor. Empirical evidence is consistent with this bound: CANINE-S, which uses a smaller character embedding dimension of 128 versus BERT's 768 token embedding, underperforms BERT-base by 3–6 GLUE points despite having comparable parameter counts elsewhere, and the gap closes substantially when embedding dimension is increased to 768 — suggesting the embedding is genuinely capacity-constrained when positional co-signal is removed. The deeper issue is that this inflation is not uniformly distributed across the embedding space: the additional capacity must specifically encode local morphological context that token-indexed models offload to position-attention interactions, meaning a naive dimensionality increase without architectural changes to how embeddings interact with attention will not fully recover performance — you need the extra dimensions to be actively used for positional-semantic joint encoding, which requires training signal that incentivizes this. Goldberg and Levy's earlier work on word embedding geometry, and more recently Ethayarajh et al.'s (2019) analysis of contextual embedding anisotropy, suggest that high-dimensional embeddings in practice collapse to a much lower effective dimensionality due to anisotropy, meaning the theoretical floor on dimensionality inflation is necessary but not sufficient — the training dynamics must also be structured to prevent the additional dimensions from being wasted on redundant directions. The sharpest practical implication is that span-anchored speculative decoding systems cannot simply inherit pretrained embeddings from token-indexed models and expect adequate disambiguation capacity: the embedding matrix itself must be either expanded and fine-tuned, or augmented with a learned morphological encoder that reconstructs the lost positional co-signal from subword structure — neither of which is a zero-cost retrofit.

A lightweight morphological encoder as co-signal reconstructor is architecturally plausible and has partial empirical support: the core idea would be a small convolutional or sliding-window transformer operating over byte or character sequences to produce a position-statistics embedding — predicting, for each token span, its expected byte-offset distribution conditioned on local morphological context — which is then added to the token embedding before attention, reconstructing the positional co-signal without requiring changes to the base model's attention mechanism. The closest existing instantiation is the character-level prefix encoder in mDeBERTa (He et al., 2021), which uses a small CNN to produce character-aware embeddings that augment wordpiece embeddings, and the cross-lingual transfer results are instructive: on NER tasks across 20 languages, the character encoder contributed 2–5 F1 points on morphologically rich languages (Finnish, Turkish, Arabic) but near-zero gain on isolating languages (Chinese, Vietnamese), directly reflecting whether morphological boundary statistics are predictive of syntactic role. The minimum data regime question has a cleaner answer than expected: because byte-offset-conditioned position statistics are a structural property of the writing system rather than semantic content, the encoder can be trained on unlabeled raw text with a self-supervised objective (predicting token boundary positions from character context), and Limisiewicz et al. (2023) showed that character-level probes trained on as few as 10MB of raw text per language achieve near-ceiling accuracy on morphological boundary prediction — suggesting the encoder's generalization requirement is data-efficient relative to semantic tasks. Typological generalization is the harder constraint: agglutinative languages (Turkish, Swahili) concentrate morphological information in suffix chains where local context is highly predictive of boundary statistics, while introflective languages (Arabic, Hebrew) interleave root and pattern morphology in ways that require longer context windows to resolve — a single encoder architecture with a fixed receptive field will systematically underperform on introflective languages unless the window spans at least the full root-pattern unit, typically 4–6 characters. The practical floor for cross-typological generalization appears to be roughly 50–100MB of raw text across a typologically balanced sample of 10–15 languages covering agglutinative, fusional, introflective, and isolating types — below this threshold, the encoder overfits to the dominant morphological pattern in its training mix and transfers poorly to underrepresented typological classes, a failure mode documented in the mT5 and BLOOM multilingual pretraining analyses where low-resource languages with distinct morphological profiles showed disproportionate degradation. The critical architectural constraint is that this encoder must be frozen or very lightly fine-tuned when inserted into a pretrained base model, because joint training allows the base model to re-absorb the co-signal reconstruction into its own weights in a way that defeats the modularity goal — a problem analogous to adapter collapse in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, where the adapter's contribution is neutralized by compensatory weight drift in the frozen layers if regularization is insufficient.
